title: Japanese From Afar
bodyHtml:
Flag semaphore is a technique that uses flags to communicate, best known for enabling sailors to talk across long distances. Below are several Japanese words written in three different ways: in a standard Japanese script called katakana, in the Latin script (the same set of letters that are used to write English), and in the Japanese version of flag semaphore. Definitions are also provided, but they are not needed to solve the problem. Knowledge of Japanese is also not needed.

KatakanaLatin ScriptJapanese Flag SemaphoreDefinition
ノミnomi3 flag figures (see image above)flea
アフリカafurika5 flag figures (see image above)Africa
コモロkomoro5 flag figures (see image above)Comoros
アイツaitsu5 flag figures (see image above)that person
ナオミnaomi6 flag figures (see image above)Naomi

E1. Below, numbered (i) through (vii), there are several more katakana characters along with their equivalents in the Latin script. Match each of these to the correct Japanese Flag Semaphore example from A through H. Each of your answers should be written as one letter (A, B, C, D, E, F, G, or H). Be warned: one of these eight letters will remain unused!

i) テ te    ii) ヨ yo    iii) ア a    iv) ミ mi    v) モ mo    vi) ヌ nu    vii) セ se

E2. The letter that was not used in E1 corresponds to one of the characters below. Which one?

メ me    ヰ wi    ク ku    ヘ he    ホ ho    シ si

assets.alt: Table of five Japanese words. Each row gives the katakana spelling, the Latin-script spelling, a sequence of Japanese flag-semaphore figures (stick figures holding one dark flag and one light flag in various arm positions), and an English definition.
Grid of eight lettered semaphore options A through H, arranged in two rows (A-D on top, E-H below). Each option shows two flag-semaphore figures side by side.

questions.partPrompt: Match each katakana character to the correct Japanese Flag Semaphore example from A through H. One letter will remain unused.
The letter that was not used in E1 corresponds to one of the characters below. Which one?
questions.promptHtml: Choose the katakana character that the leftover semaphore signal stands for.

hints.text: Start by counting. Count how many flag figures each word uses, and compare that with how many katakana characters the word has. The numbers do not match, so a single katakana character can take more than one flag figure.

Some katakana characters appear in more than one word in the table. If two words begin (or end) with the same character, their semaphore signals must begin (or end) with the same figures — that lets you cut the long strings of figures into per-character chunks. Notice too that every lettered option A–H is made of exactly two figures, so you are only looking for two-figure characters.

Worked example with a character that is NOT one of the graded items: ノミ (nomi) has only three flag figures for two characters, so one character uses one figure and the other uses two. ノ is written with a single sweeping stroke, and sure enough the very first figure of ノミ holds its flags out along one diagonal line — the same slant as the stroke of ノ. So ノ = one figure, and the remaining two figures belong to ミ. Use that same trick to peel characters off the beginnings and ends of the other words.

explanationHtml:
What flag semaphore is doing here

In flag semaphore, a signaller holds a flag in each hand and puts their arms into different positions. Each little stick figure in this problem is one arm position (one flag dark, one flag light). The Japanese version does not spell sounds letter by letter the way the international one does: it builds up katakana characters out of one, two or three arm positions, and the arm positions imitate the strokes you would draw to write the character.

Step 1: count figures and count characters

Line up the words with how many flag figures each one uses:

WordKatakana charactersFlag figures
ノミ nomi23
アフリカ afurika45
コモロ komoro35
アイツ aitsu35
ナオミ naomi36

There are always more figures than characters, so one character can need more than one figure. Also important: every lettered option A–H consists of exactly two figures. So all eight options are two-figure characters, and each of the seven characters in E1 must occupy two figures somewhere.

Step 2: use repeated characters to cut the strings apart

This is the key move. Several characters show up twice in the table:

  • ア starts both アフリカ and アイツ → the two words must begin with the same figures. Compare the first figures of those two rows: the first two figures are identical in both. That pair of figures is ア. Now look through A–H for that pair — it is option D.
  • ミ ends both ノミ and ナオミ → the last figures of those two rows match. Since ノ takes just one figure (see below), ミ must be the last two figures of ノミ, and the same pair sits at the end of ナオミ. That pair is option H.

How do we know ノ takes only one figure? ノミ has three figures for two characters, and we already learned that ミ is a two-figure character, so ノ gets exactly one. That fits its shape: ノ is a single diagonal stroke, and its figure holds both flags along one slanted line.

Once ミ is settled, subtract it from ナオミ (6 figures − 2 = 4 figures left for ナ + オ, so two each), and subtract ア from アフリカ (5 − 2 = 3 figures for フ, リ, カ — one each). In コモロ, モ is a two-figure character, so it accounts for two of the five figures, leaving three for コ and ロ. Finding the two figures of モ inside that row and looking them up in the option grid gives option C.

Step 3: characters that are not in the table

テ, ヨ, ヌ and セ never appear in the five words, so you cannot read them off directly. Instead, treat the individual figures as a small alphabet of stroke shapes that you have now learned from the words: a flag held straight out to the side draws a horizontal stroke, a flag held on a slant draws a diagonal, a flag raised high draws a stroke that starts at the top, and so on. Then decompose each unknown character into its strokes and hunt for the option whose two figures draw exactly those strokes in that order:

  • テ te — a pair of horizontals over a downward stroke → option A
  • ヨ yo — stacked horizontals hanging from a right-hand edge → option E
  • ヌ nu — a horizontal plus a long diagonal sweep → option F
  • セ se — a horizontal crossed by a rising stroke → option B

Putting E1 together: i) テ = A, ii) ヨ = E, iii) ア = D, iv) ミ = H, v) モ = C, vi) ヌ = F, vii) セ = B.

Step 4: the leftover option (E2)

Every letter is used except G. Notice that G shares one of its two figures with E, the signal for ヨ yo — so G should be a character built on the same shape as ヨ, with one extra stroke. Of the six candidates (メ me, ヰ wi, ク ku, ヘ he, ホ ho, シ si), the one whose shape is essentially ヨ with an extra vertical stroke is ヰ wi (an old katakana character, no longer used in modern Japanese). So the answer to E2 is ヰ wi.

Takeaway

The general strategy is the one linguists use on any unknown script: you cannot decode a symbol in isolation, but repeated items let you segment a long signal into pieces, and once you have pieces you can look for a systematic relationship between the pieces and the shapes (or sounds) they represent.

(1) 2024-open-e-data-table.png: the whole 5-row data table (Katakana / Latin Script / Japanese Flag Semaphore / Definition), roughly the middle third of the page, just below the intro paragraph — MUST include the full semaphore column so figure sequences stay aligned with their rows. (2) 2024-open-e-options.png: the 2x4 grid of lettered semaphore options A-D (top row) and E-H (bottom row), just below the i)-vii) character list. The semaphore stick figures cannot be transcribed as text, so the images are essential; the text table in bodyHtml only repeats katakana/Latin/definition and the figure counts. Answer keys for E1 (A, E, D, H, C, F, B) and E2 (ヰ wi) are taken directly from the official solution page. Point split (1 point per E1 item, 3 for E2) is my allocation of the 10 official points — the official sheet gives no per-part breakdown. The stroke-by-stroke reasoning in the explanation (which figure draws which stroke, and the ヨ/ヰ shared-element argument in Step 4) is my reconstruction of the semaphore system from the data, not quoted from an official commentary; please sanity-check it against the figures when cropping.
